item.title: 'We abide by the one-China principle,' Naoero's President tells GT
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-16 00:20:00
After tasting apples grown by local farmers, the delegation led by Naoero's President David Adeang picks them up to take photos as souvenirs during a visit to Liangjiahe in Yan'an, Shaanxi Province, on November 15, 2026. Photo: Meng Xu/Global Times Naoero's President David Adeang visited the remote village of Liangjiahe in the hills of Northwest China's Shaanxi Province on Sunday, where President Xi Jinping once lived and worked as an "educated youth." After wrapping up his schedule for the day, Adeang told the media he was deeply impressed by the tour. This is Adeang's second visit to China in 2026. During his trip to Shaanxi, he also toured the Yangjialing Revolutionary Site, Baota Mountain and other locations to learn about the history of the CPC. President Adeang on Saturday laid a flower basket for Huangdi, or the Yellow Emperor, the cultural ancestor of the Chinese nation, becoming the first foreign leader to pay homage at the Yellow Emperor's Mausoleum. "I am the President of Naoero. My responsibility is to build a closer relationship between our two countries. The more I understand and learn about China, the better I can improve the relations between our two countries," he said in an exclusive interview with the Global Times. Talking about progress since the resumption of diplomatic ties in 2024, Adeang said "Naoero's economic and social development have been almost transformed." A section of history that can be 'tasted' Liangjiahe is a small village located on the Loess Plateau where President Xi spent nearly 7 years since 1969. During his visit, Adeang learned about the Chinese leader's youth in the village and the transformations that have occurred over the past several decades through pictures and real objects on display at the village museum. Adeang tried locally grown apples, which he described to the Global Times reporters as "very tasty, like a bite into history." The Naoero's president was informed that apples were not grown in the region in the past, and development used to be sluggish. However, through the efforts of President Xi, this region and the lives of local people have been transformed. Apple cultivation has now become an important and growing part of the local economy and the livelihoods of the people. "Therefore, it's a section of history that can be 'tasted,'" he remarked. The trip to Yan'an offered Adeang an opportunity to gain further insight into the history of the CPC and its vital role in China's development. He said the tour in Shaanxi has given him a deeper understanding of the Chinese people and the Chinese system. For him, these gains are extremely valuable as he is committed to continuously advancing the relationship between the two countries, he noted. First foreign leader to pay homage at the Yellow Emperor's Mausoleum Another import stop on Adeang's visit was the Yellow Emperor's Mausoleum. In a solemn ceremony, Adeang and his delegation laid a flower basket for Huangdi, or Yellow Emperor, the cultural ancestor of the Chinese nation, and bowed three times. His two daughters joined him in presenting the flower basket. For Adeang, this visit is an exploration of the deep-rooted Chinese civilization and enriches the cultural implications of his special connection with China. Over 100 years ago, some of Adeang's ancestors departed from Jiangmen, South China's Guangdong Province, in the 19th century for Southeast Asia to make a living and eventually settled in Naoero. In July 2025, Adeang visited Jiangmen with his family to trace his family roots, pay respects to his ancestors, visit relatives and plant a tree signifying family bonds. In February 2026, he brought his daughter to Jiangmen to celebrate the Spring Festival. After learning about his nicknames on Chinese internet, including "President cousin," Adeang told the Global Times with a smile that it is about affection, respect, and "also reflects where I want to take the relationship between our two countries. It is not only close friends, but even closer." 'New opportunities and prospects' found in every visit If Adeang's century-spanning family story has forged a special emotional bond between him and China, the deepening practical cooperation since the two countries resumed diplomatic ties has laid a more solid and tangible foundation for this friendship across the Pacific. Naoero announced its recognition of the one-China principle and severed "diplomatic relations" with Taiwan authorities in January 2024. On January 24, China and Naoero signed a joint communique in Beijing on the resumption of diplomatic relations at the ambassadorial level, the Xinhua News Agency reported. Talking about that important decision, Adeang reaffirmed that the one-China principle is central to bilateral relationship. "We respect that and abide by it." Since the resumption of bilateral relations, the Naoero's economy and social development have been almost transformed. "I say 'almost' because it has been only two years and there is much more to come," Adeang noted. The prospects are becoming concrete and clear in every cooperation project. In Naoero, a China-aid sports center is taking shape, and Chinese medical experts traveled across the ocean in September to treat more than 300 patients, providing nearly 500 traditional Chinese medicine consultations and services. Adeang also experienced acupuncture and cupping therapy. The Chinese Embassy in Naoero told the Global Times that rapid progress in bilateral cooperation cannot be made without solid mutual political trust. Since the resumption of diplomatic ties, Naoero has consistently committed to the one-China principle, reaffirming its stance publicly multiple times and upholding it with concrete actions. In May, the Naoero's government issued a directive to all public servants and employees of state-owned enterprises to adhere to the one-China principle. In July 2026, China successfully conducted the test launch of a strategic missile by a submarine in the high seas of the Pacific Ocean, which was a routine arrangement of annual military training and complied with international law and international practice; however, it rattled some ill-intentioned Western countries. They not only made unwarranted remarks about China's move but also ganged up to condemn it. Against this backdrop, Naoero has taken an impartial stance and spoken up for China. During this year's Pacific Islands Forum Leaders' Meeting, Naoero dissented against the adoption of a statement that contains innuendos against China. Previously expressing his hope to visit China at least once a year, Adeang told the Global Times that his intentions are not solely about family bonds. Whenever Adeang and his cabinet come to China, they are impressed by the range of new opportunities and prospects. "It is an exciting relationship. We hope and intend to maximize its potential," Adeang noted.

item.title: Once again, China's youth are 'stepping up to the plate'!: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-15 22:30:00
China's youth have become trailblazers Illustration:Xia Qing/GT From the pioneers of the "Two Bombs, One Satellite" program who blazed a trail through the Gobi Desert, to today's youth taking up the torch to tackle challenges in various emerging fields, what has changed is the arena, but what remains unchanged is the innate spirit of never giving up and daring to strive - a spirit ingrained in the blood of the Chinese people. Today's Chinese youth possess greater confidence and capability. Rather than settling for being followers, they have become trailblazers setting trends in emerging new frontier sectors. The 2026 League of Legends World Championship concluded in New York in the early hours of November 15, Beijing Time. Chinese team, Bilibili Gaming (BLG), defeated South Korea's Gen.G to claim the championship title in this esports tournament, which boasts the largest global participation and the highest level of competition. Related topics immediately went viral across major domestic social media platforms, while media from multiple countries rushed to cover the event. Esports is an arena for the young. The average age of BLG's players is early 20s, and the tournament's core audience also consists largely of young people. By fully showcasing their talents on the global stage, they have not only raised the international profile of China's youth but also opened a window into the world of today's young people. BLG's road to the title was, in many ways, a battle to prove its doubters wrong. Before the tournament, much of the global esports community had little faith in the competitiveness of China's League of Legends teams, and BLG itself had an underwhelming group-stage performance. But after advancing to the knockout stage, the team first defeated South Korea's T1, a powerhouse that had maintained an unbeaten record against Chinese teams for 13 years. Then, despite falling behind early in the final, BLG fought back to overcome Gen.G, the top seed from the South Korean league and one of the tournament favorites. In doing so, it helped dispel the long-standing perception that Chinese teams were unable to overcome their South Korean rivals. A documentary released by the club after the victory offered a glimpse into what it took to reach the top. It showed players enduring years of repetitive, demanding training during their academy days, as well as the difficult periods when the team struggled and few believed in its prospects. Clips from the documentary quickly spread across social media. BLG's determination to push through setbacks and prove its critics wrong has struck a chord with young people, many of whom share a desire to challenge prejudice and let their achievements speak for themselves. Looking beyond the esports arena, there is a much broader world where the younger generation is also making its mark. The DeepSeek team consists of fewer than 140 people, with an average age of about 28; more than 75 percent were born in the 1990s, and over half were born after 1995. For the "Beidou" satellite network, the average age of the satellite development team was 31. For the "Chang'e" lunar soil sampling mission, the average age of the heads of key telemetry, tracking, and command positions was 33. For the "Tiangong" space station construction, the average age of the Mengtian lab module final assembly team was 33. And for the "Tianwen" Mars exploration mission, the average age of the flight control team was just 30. A former administrator of the US National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) once remarked publicly that one of China's space program's greatest strengths lies in the large number of young scientists and engineers it possesses. The Washington Post also noted that "while China's older tech pioneers tend to idolize Silicon Valley," China's younger generation find their role models in people such as DeepSeek's Liang Wenfeng and Unitree's Wang Xingxing. The fact that China's young people are capable of shouldering major responsibilities is winning admiration across the world. For a long time, the ideals of solidarity, hard work and bringing honor to the country were most commonly associated with traditional sports, factory floors, laboratories and fields across the country. But as the digital economy has grown rapidly, a new generation of young Chinese has come of age in new emerging fields, including esports, e-commerce, livestreaming, trendy Chinese cultural products, AI, and green energy. These fields share a common characteristic: rapid knowledge evolution and a high density of innovation. Unlike traditional sectors that require long-term experience and expertise, in these emerging fields, young people often have an edge due to their familiarity with new rules and their sensitivity to technological trends. They do not have to follow the paths paved by their predecessors to the letter; instead, they can compete directly with their global peers on newly opened tracks, and even overtake them by leveraging more flexible thinking and stronger learning abilities. From the pioneers of the "Two Bombs, One Satellite" program (China's successful detonation of an atomic bomb, its first intercontinental ballistic missile, and its first artificial satellite) who blazed a trail through the Gobi Desert, to today's youth taking up the torch to tackle challenges in various emerging fields, what has changed is the arena, but what remains unchanged is the innate spirit of never giving up and daring to strive - a spirit ingrained in the blood of the Chinese people. In the past, when people spoke of "stepping up to the plate," they often referred to hardship, sacrifice, and perseverance. Today's young Chinese not only embody these qualities, but also demonstrate the poise to engage with the world on equal footing, alongside an open-minded and collaborative spirit. Supported by decades of popularized basic education, expanded higher education access, sustained growth in R&D investment, and the accumulated strengths of a complete industrial system, today's Chinese youth possess greater confidence and capability. Rather than settling for being followers, they have become trailblazers setting trends in emerging new frontier sectors. As more and more teams, whose members average in their 20s and 30s, step into the spotlight of the world's top fields, the future of this nation naturally gains its most solid foundation. What the outside world sees in BLG's championship victory is not only the triumph of one esports team, but also the ambition, vigor, and confidence of a nation's younger generation. The vibrant, upward-striving energy of youth is precisely the moving underlying force driving China's continuous progress.

item.title: GT Voice: US chip curb debate cannot stymie China's AI progress
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-15 22:13:00
Production of semiconductor chip File photo: VCG Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corp (SMIC), China's largest contract chipmaker, reported a 123.4 percent year-on-year increase in net profit attributable to shareholders in the third quarter of 2026. Its performance reflects a broader trend in China's semiconductor industry, where growing market demand is translating into stronger commercial returns. Even if Washington tightens chip export restrictions further, China's artificial intelligence (AI) industry now rests on a firmer industrial foundation than a few years ago. Jensen Huang's resignation as Nvidia's CEO has sparked intense debate in recent days over its implications for US technology policy. Some observers said that his exit could weaken the chip industry's influence in Washington. Given that many American chip companies have argued that their products should be allowed into China on commercial grounds, Huang's resignation could leave those commercial interests with a less influential voice in Washington, giving greater sway to overblown national security arguments that are increasingly influencing US technology policy. The political tug-of-war over US chip exports to China has been intense in Washington, but its impact on China's AI development may prove increasingly limited. Years of tightening export controls have accelerated China's efforts to build an AI industry that can stand on its own, with far less reliance on American chips. The result is an industry increasingly capable of moving forward without access to American technology. This resilience is built in China thanks to many years' strenuous efforts by Chinese companies. Huawei, Cambricon and other Chinese chipmakers are constantly expanding their presence in the market, while Chinese technology companies are adapting their AI models and computing systems to a growing range of homegrown processors. Together, these developments are giving China an increasingly self-sustaining AI computing ecosystem, making the industry less vulnerable to external restrictions and less dependent on access to US technology. An important part of this picture is China's AI boom, which is opening up new commercial opportunities for its technology industry, including Chinese chipmakers. As demand grows, companies across the semiconductor supply chain have a massive market to expand their businesses and invest in research, development and innovation. SMIC, for instance, spent $258.4 million on research and development in the third quarter alone. This creates a virtuous cycle: the expanding AI market gives domestic chipmakers greater space to grow, generating revenues and profits that can be ploughed back into R&D. Such investment strengthens China's semiconductor industry and, in turn, supports its broader AI development. The progress China's AI industry has made in recent years demonstrates the strength of this cycle, even as the US has tightened its chip restrictions. The harder Washington tightens its technology restrictions, the more complicated the consequences could bring to the US itself. Reuters reported on Friday that Southeast Asia's chip and data center industries expect greater US scrutiny as Washington considers extending export controls. Whether or not these reports translate into policy, the possibility of broader US controls could prompt more Asian economies to reassess their dependence on American technology and accelerate their efforts to diversify their supply chains. This could create new opportunities for Chinese chipmakers, as regional economies seek to broaden their source of chip supplies. And, there could be growing difficulties facing Nvidia and other US chipmakers in the years to come. The growing uncertainty surrounding American chip export controls is increasingly becoming a burden on the industry Washington seeks to "protect." It is also a predicament that post-Huang's Nvidia has to confront. The semiconductor industry is built on deeply intertwined supply chains. Further US export controls could affect chipmakers and technology sectors in Asia, including China, but US companies may be among the first to bear the cost. Whatever the noises Washington makes, China's AI industry will move forward and keep gathering pace. Global Times

item.title: Chinese scientists identify 'fairy circles' in northern China's drylands for the first time and propose how they form
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-15 21:43:00
Fairy circles photographed by the research team near Alxa Left Banner, North China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region Photo: Courtesy of Yu Kailiang Chinese scientists have recently identified fairy circles, unusual ring-shaped patterns with sparse vegetation or bare in centers, for the first time in northern China's arid regions and used phase transition theory from statistical physics to explain how the circles may have formed in these drylands, the Global Times learned from the research group on Sunday. The joint research conducted by the research team led by Yu Guirui, an academician of the Institute of Geographic Sciences and Natural Resources Research, Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS), in collaboration with researchers from the Lanzhou University and Gansu Agricultural University, was published in the international academic journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS) on November 11 local time. Found in the arid regions of Namibia and Australia, fairy circles are unusual ring-shaped patterns in which vegetation flourishes around the edges but is sparse or absent in the center. In China, previous fairy circle research had focused largely on coastal salt marshes, with no confirmed existence in arid and semi-arid regions. The research team studied precipitation gradients along the edges of sandy areas and deserts in northern China, used drones to capture high-resolution images and conducted field surveys. They discovered these patterns, formed by hollow rings of shrubs, at the boundaries between shrublands and grasslands. According to Sun Jingyao, first author of the research paper and postdoctoral researcher at the Institute of Geographic Sciences and Natural Resources Research, the discovery marks the first confirmed record of fairy circles in China's arid regions, alongside with the mechanisms behind their formation being identified as well. Challenging conventional explanations that attribute fairy circles to termite activity or biomass-water feedbacks, the study applies phase transition theory to ecology, suggesting that the patterns emerge naturally when ecosystems reach a critical state, Sun said. Sun explained that phase transition theory, a branch of physics, examines abrupt changes in matter as it shifts from one state or phase to another, and the critical behavior associated with these changes. The researchers used mathematical modeling to demonstrate that fairy circles represent a spatially partitioned "metastable state" in which shrubs and grasses coexist amid intense competition for resources. Sun explained that as precipitation increases and competition from grasses intensifies, the centers of shrub patches become bare due to water scarcity, forming hollow spaces. These hollow rings, in turn, help collect water and sustain the survival of the shrubs. Phase transition theory enables researchers to explain fairy circles and look for early warning signs of ecological collapse along desert margins. Yu Kailiang, corresponding author of the research paper and a research fellow at the institute, told the Global Times on Sunday that fairy circles and vegetation patch expansion were previously treated as isolated natural phenomena and studied separately. However, this study links these phenomena through physical principles, demonstrating that seemingly different abrupt ecological shifts are all manifestations of the same underlying organizational mechanism. It also offers a testable framework for identifying spatial warning signs of potential ecosystem collapse, Yu said.

item.title: APEC CEO Summit draws 115 Fortune Global 500 firms
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-15 21:00:00
The media center for the 2026 APEC Economic Leaders' Week holds a special briefing on November 16, 2026. The picture shows an APEC official at the media center displaying an English special issue of the meeting. Photo: VCG Representatives from 115 Fortune Global 500 companies will attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) CEO Summit in Shenzhen, South China's Guangdong Province, on November 17 and 18, the China Council for the Promotion of International Trade (CCPIT) said on Sunday. This turnout reflects businesses across the region seeking new opportunities and stability for cross-border trade amid rising protectionism. The summit is expected to host more than 2,000 participants from business, government and the media. Twelve leaders of Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation economies will attend the APEC CEO Summit 2026. Heads of international organizations and business associations from economies including the US, Russia and Japan are also expected to attend, a spokesperson from the CCPIT said. The breadth of participation highlights one of APEC's strengths, Hu Qimu, a professor at the Maritime Silk Road Institute of Huaqiao University, told the Global Times. It brings together the world's two largest economies alongside both developed and developing economies at different stages of growth. "Industries at different stages of development, markets of different types, and economies of varying sizes can all find opportunities for cooperation," Hu said. China's APEC host year focuses on openness, innovation and cooperation, under the theme "To Prosper and Win the Future Together." The CEO Summit agenda will address critical topics such as the proposed Free Trade Area of the Asia-Pacific, connectivity, the digital economy and sustainable development. These discussions build on substantial trade ties. In the first three quarters of 2026, China's trade with other APEC economies rose by 23.9 percent year on year to 24.07 trillion yuan ($3.6 trillion), accounting for 60.3 percent of its total foreign trade, customs data showed. This will mark the third time China hosts the APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting, following Shanghai in 2001 and Beijing in 2014. Former Singaporean foreign minister George Yeo told the Global Times that holding the meeting in Shenzhen was "symbolically important." He noted that it underscores China's commitment to reform and opening-up while also highlighting the development of the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area. For businesses, Hu noted that bringing policymakers and executives together provides an opportunity for economies with different development priorities to identify overlapping commercial interests. Firms eye China US companies make up the largest group among participating firms from outside China, accounting for nearly one-fifth of the total, according to the CCPIT. The South China Morning Post reported that Google and Boeing have confirmed places in the US business delegation. The CCPIT said in September that Amazon, Walmart, Apple, ExxonMobil and Microsoft were among the US companies that had applied to attend. Recent earnings reports show the scale of the Chinese market for these companies. Apple's net sales in the Chinese mainland, Taiwan, Hong Kong and Macao reached $17.54 billion in the fiscal quarter ending September 26, up 21 percent year on year. Walmart reported $7.42 billion in net sales in China for the quarter ending July 31, up 28.2 percent. Boeing has identified China as a significant market for commercial aircraft in its latest quarterly filing. He Weiwen, a senior fellow at the Center for China and Globalization, told the Global Times that the strong presence of US companies at the summit can be attributed to two factors. First, the size of the US economy within APEC accounts for the representation of many of its largest companies. He noted a similar pattern at the China International Import Expo, where US companies have maintained a large presence for several years. What is particularly noteworthy this time, He said, is that the two countries' leaders have set a direction for a more constructive and stable relationship, encouraging US companies to engage with their counterparts. They are coming to Shenzhen "to look for more business opportunities," with an eye on both the Chinese market and the wider Asia-Pacific region. The summit will also attract companies from 13 economies outside APEC, including the UK, France, Germany and Switzerland. Among Asia-Pacific firms, Thailand's Charoen Pokphand Group has applied to attend. Its listed food business, Charoen Pokphand Foods, reported that higher earnings from associates following the restructuring of its feed and swine operations in China helped lift third-quarter net profit attributable to shareholders by about 1 percent year on year to 5.23 billion baht ($154.39 million). Hu said the appeal for businesses across economies lies in the concentration of some of the world's most dynamic markets in the Asia-Pacific. Companies from different industries can use the same forum to find partners and explore opportunities across multiple markets. Yeo provided a Southeast Asian perspective, saying that ASEAN values its friendship with China and that China understands the grouping's desire to maintain ties with all major powers. That flexibility allows Southeast Asian economies the room to pursue commercial ties with a range of partners. Business policy input At the fourth meeting of the APEC Business Advisory Council (ABAC), business representatives from China and the US jointly proposed strengthening Asia-Pacific supply-chain cooperation, while Chinese and Canadian representatives submitted an "AI plus" proposal, Wu Meng, head of the CCPIT's international cooperation department, said on Sunday. These proposals demonstrate how businesses can collaborate across borders and bring shared concerns to policymakers through APEC. "Maintaining the integrity and resilience of supply chains across APEC economies is in the interests of businesses," He Weiwen said, warning that political pressure in Washington to restrict technology flows could fragment supply chains that extend well beyond China and the US, ultimately affecting businesses in Southeast Asia as well. A joint proposal from the two business communities, he said, shows that companies still see value in keeping those networks connected. In his view, the CEO Summit can amplify this shared interest, providing a stronger voice as governments consider trade and technology policies. Against the rise of trade protectionism, China has put shared prosperity at the center of the Shenzhen meetings. The theme "To Prosper and Win the Future Together" reflects this emphasis on mutual benefit. The business community will have a concrete way to contribute, as ABAC presents recommendations directly to APEC leaders, and the CEO Summit will draw on the council's work and its own discussions to issue a Shenzhen Initiative. "Across the Asia-Pacific, it is easier to find common ground on economic and trade issues," Hu said. APEC provides members with differing political positions the opportunity to make progress. Closer ties among producers and suppliers can in turn give those economies a greater stake in keeping trade channels open. Hu said keeping the discussion focused on economic cooperation is particularly important when geopolitical disagreements complicate the ability to reach consensus. For the wider Asia-Pacific, He said, the Shenzhen summit offers businesses a platform to advocate for the maintenance of connected regional supply chains as trade barriers rise. "This summit is a positive force. It can help counter the trend toward geopolitical fragmentation," He said.

item.title: China's AI study tours gain traction during autumn school breaks, but should prioritize sustained learning over operating high-tech products: expert
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-15 20:49:00
Primary school students visit an artificial intelligence education center in Handan, North China's Hebei Province, to explore AI technologies on November 12, 2026. Photo: VCG As autumn school breaks arrive in several parts of China during mid-November,study tours featuring artificial intelligence (AI), robotics and other emerging technologies have become increasingly popular, sparking discussions on whether such programs should go beyond letting children operate high-tech products. Across China, a growing range of activities is bringing emerging technologies closer to younger generations, turning industrial bases, museums and science centers into classrooms beyond school walls. At an embodied intelligence industrial base in Jinan, East China's Shandong Province, students can put on VR headsets and use motion-capture devices to control robotic arms to pick up objects, while watching humanoid robots write calligraphy and make coffee. The base estimated that it would receive more than 5,000 young visitors during the autumn break and the following weekend, making a period record since it began offering study programs. In Qingdao, also in Shandong, a science carnival organized by the city's academy of young scientists attracted more than 2,000 students with 12 interactive challenges and six full inquiry-based courses, according to the local education bureau. For some parents, such experiences offer children an opportunity to look beyond conventional classroom learning and get an early glimpse of future technological developments. Qiu Shuhua, a mother of a middle school student in East China's Jiangsu Province, told the Global Times on Sunday that while their generation's study tours were often about sightseeing and learning history, today's children have opportunities to explore AI, large language models and AI agents at technology events. Although children may not fully understand these technologies yet, close encounters with the latest developments can gradually broaden their horizons and help them imagine the future, Qiu said. "One generation's study tours were about looking back at history; the next generation's are about facing the future," she added. Li Qingdu, an AI and robotics researcher and educator, told the Global Times that AI study programs should help students understand the underlying logic of artificial intelligence and develop problem-solving skills through practice, rather than simply allowing them to operate technological products. Li suggested that programs for young learners should cover core aspects of AI, including perception, reasoning, learning, decision-making and interaction, while helping students recognize the technology's capabilities and limitations. AI study tours have developed rapidly only over the past three years, and their educational frameworks are still immature, cautioning against excessive reliance on such programs, Li noted. As AI becomes increasingly integrated into everyday life, some parents are also considering how to introduce the technology to children in an age-appropriate and guided way. Science-oriented activities that combine hands-on learning with professional explanations can offer another approach. Su Zizhou, a mother of an elementary school child from Shenzhen, South China's Guangdong Province, told the Global Times that they took their child to Shanghai Science and Technology Museum during the autumn break for an AI-themed study program. The activities included a science and technology class, hands-on crafts and guided tours covering topics ranging from rainforest ecosystems to astronomy. Beyond AI-focused programs, other institutions have also used the school break to encourage broader scientific exploration. The Jiangsu Science and Technology Museum, for example, organized science experiment shows, maker activities, science crafts and interactive programs from November 6 to 10.

item.title: Chinese firm unveils world's first fully integrated analog chip for one-step matrix solving
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-15 20:46:00
Anatrix's AX100 analog computing chip Photo: Screenshot of the Science and Technology Daily's report Chinese chip developer Anatrix has unveiled the AX100, which it describes as the world's first fully integrated analog computing chip capable of solving matrix equations in a single step. The chip completed tape-out in October and solved a matrix equation in under 100 nanoseconds in tests, the Science and Technology Daily reported on Sunday. Matrix equations help AI models learn, robots adjust their movements and mobile base stations process signals. Conventional digital chips typically solve these equations through a series of calculations. The AX100 represents an equation as an electrical circuit and reads the answer once the circuit settles into equilibrium, Xiang Rui, the company's CEO, said in the report. Anatrix tested the chip in three areas. In AI experiments involving two models, the method tested with the chip cut the computing cost of updating model parameters by 92 percent and 56 percent, respectively. In embodied AI, tests showed faster motion control and route planning, which could help robots respond more quickly as their surroundings change. In wireless communications, the company's evaluation found that the chip could process more data with the same amount of energy than the digital chips and GPUs used for comparison on a specific signal-processing task. The AX100 brings research published by a Peking University team in Nature Electronics in October 2025 onto a chip in about a year. The company said the chip can be manufactured using mature production processes, offering a way to accelerate some computing tasks that currently run on digital chips using existing manufacturing technology, according to the report. Global Times

item.title: HSK candidates top 1 mln amid growing interest in Chinese language driven by employment, business and industry needs
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-15 20:40:00
The 2026 World Chinese Language Conference is held at the China National Convention Center in Beijing from November 13 to 15, bringing together around 5,000 representatives from more than 160 countries and regions. Photo: VCG The number of candidates taking the Chinese Proficiency Test (HSK) surpassed 1 million for the first time in 2026, reflecting growing global interest in learning Chinese, China Central Television (CCTV) News reported Sunday. The language is increasingly becoming a practical tool for employment, cross-border business and industrial cooperation, educators told the Global Times. The milestone was announced during the 2026 World Chinese Language Conference, held in Beijing from November 13 to 15, which brought together around 5,000 representatives from more than 160 countries and regions. Similar to TOEFL or IELTS for foreign applicants to universities in English-speaking countries, HSK has established more than 1,500 test centers in 169 countries, the widest country coverage among global language proficiency tests. It has served more than 9 million test-takers cumulatively. Meanwhile, the number of people overseas learning and using Chinese has reached 210 million. The growing demand is also reflected in the changing profiles of learners. Adult Chinese courses in New York have expanded rapidly in recent years, attracting not only beginners but also students who have reached HSK Level 5 or 6 and even higher, Cheng Dahai, co-founder of a Chinese language learning and testing center in Manhattan, New York, told CCTV News. Some students are increasingly interested in gaining a deeper understanding of industries such as science and technology and manufacturing, while acquiring the specialized vocabulary needed to work in these fields, Cheng said. Li Xiaobing, founder of AI Chinese, an online Chinese-learning platform, told the Global Times that the 1 million HSK candidates represent only part of the global Chinese-learning market, as many people learn the language for employment at Chinese companies overseas or to conduct business with Chinese partners rather than to take proficiency tests. Data from online searches for Chinese-learning resources showed exponential growth in 2024 compared with a decade earlier, Li said. Li said the platform's model combining livestreamed lessons by international students with AI-assisted bilingual Chinese teaching had attracted substantial organic traffic. In 2025, its livestreaming sessions reached more than 15 million views across five language markets. So far in 2026, the figure has exceeded 60 million, with learners from Southeast Asia, Arabic-speaking countries, Spanish-speaking regions and English-speaking countries joining the sessions. The platform's AI Chinese app has also surpassed 100,000 monthly active users this year, a 100-fold increase from early 2025, according to Li. He identified three major trends in the market: rising demand for employment-oriented Chinese learning, growing needs among professionals involved in international trade and industrial cooperation, and continued interest in Chinese language and culture for academic and long-term educational purposes. "The biggest change is the shift from general-purpose, exam-oriented Chinese to scenario-based and industry-specific 'Chinese plus' learning," Li said. Today's learners want to speak Chinese in factories, livestreaming sessions, trade negotiations and technical exchanges, rather than simply pass a proficiency test. The trend has also drawn attention from educators at the World Chinese Language Conference. During the event, the Ministry of Education's Center for Language Education and Cooperation, together with multiple institutions, launched an initiative for a "Chinese Plus" industry-education integration partnership program, aiming to help countries cultivate local talent equipped with both knowledge in Chinese language and culture, as well as professional skills. Foreign Chinese-language teachers also see practical career opportunities as a major motivation for learners. As China's technological and economic capabilities continue to grow, more people in Indonesia, her home country, are eager to learn Chinese, said Lanlan, an Indonesian teacher of Chinese. Studying in China and mastering the language can open up more employment opportunities upon returning home, she said, adding that Chinese teachers can also earn additional income through translation and private tutoring. In her teaching, Lanlan incorporates new expressions used in contemporary China, as well as Chinese songs, stories and films, to make lessons more engaging and relevant. Another teacher, Liya, also from Indonesia, said AI-assisted teaching has helped improve the learning experience by generating scenario-based dialogues that allow foreign students to explore authentic Chinese-language situations.

item.title: The AI summit that got derailed: What Dublin reveals about Europe's waning power
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-15 19:22:00
EU Illustration: Xia Qing/GT On November 13, EU leaders gathered in Dublin for a summit the outside world had been watching closely, devoted substantially to artificial intelligence (AI). But as the summit unfolded, the Ukraine issue was abruptly thrust onto the agenda - in the wake of US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner's meeting with Zelensky the day prior to the summit - becoming the summit's main focus. European leaders had to put AI aside and discuss how to form a negotiating team and "speak with one voice" to the outside world. On the surface, the US stole the show. But looking through this disrupted agenda, we see a more authentic Europe. This is not just about an agenda being hijacked; it shows how today's Europe repeatedly wavers between "security" and "prosperity." Why did security override prosperity? Because the pain of these two issues is fundamentally different. The pain of Ukraine is immediate; it hurts today and will hurt tomorrow. Funding gaps remain, a 22nd round of sanctions is coming, and the November 26 Council meeting will require more financial discussions. The fear that the US and Russia might negotiate behind closed doors and arrange Europe's fate is a terror that cashes out instantly. By contrast, the pain of AI lies 10 to 20 years in the future. No one can accurately calculate the votes a decade from now. Discussing the future requires money, the approval of 27 member states, building gigafactories, and waiting for talent to be deployed. In a system dominated by electoral politics, distant water cannot quench immediate thirst. Yet, it is this "postponed half" that exposes the hollowing out of Europe's power. At the meeting, Ursula von der Leyen said Europe was planning €30 billion (33.07 billion US dollars) to build seven AI "Gigafactories." It sounds like a lot. But to truly gain a foothold in AI, Europe needs at least €500 billion (551.10 billion dollars). Where will this money come from? The meeting didn't say. Because the moment money is mentioned, none of the 27 countries want to pay more. The factories are still on paper. The 2023 Chips Act set a goal to capture 20% of the global market, but the industry has already declared it unattainable. Look further back: The 2000 Lisbon Strategy aimed to build the world's most competitive knowledge economy by 2010. It failed, so it was rebranded as the "Europe 2020 Strategy." When 2020 arrived, it failed again. Why? Because subsidizing farmers and saving factories wins votes; spending money on long-term competitiveness does not. Therefore, whenever it comes to fork out real money, Europe habitually retreats to "coordination." This "informal meeting" didn't even pass a concluding document. It spun its wheels all day, stuck in a loop. Europe remains wealthy and dignified, and its standard of living is high. But in the hard dimensions that dictate the world's future direction - computing power, chips, and AI models - it is retreating. It is plagued by strategic anxiety, leaving it unable to achieve seemingly clear objectives, including shaping the future security landscape. You only become this anxious when you feel you might become a pawn on the chessboard. Leverage at the negotiating table never relies on declarations; it relies on hard power. In the future global landscape, computing power and chips are the hardest currency. Falling behind in this domain means losing a seat in future great power competition. A Europe that cannot stand firmly on its own feet will be entangled in immediate crises, unable to see the long-term direction, and will become more conservative, inward-looking, and more right-wing and extreme. This is hardly good news for a multipolar world. Whether Europe can maintain its strategic autonomy, strive to become a significant force in a multipolar world, and play an independent role in the international order without depending on any third party depends on how much effort it is willing to devote to these goals. What Europe lacks most is not another declaration of "strategic autonomy," but the admission that it is no longer the old, high-and-mighty Europe. It needs reform, openness, and renewed vitality. However, the agenda in Dublin - so easily derailed by Ukraine - demonstrates that taking this crucial first step remains incredibly difficult.

item.title: ASEAN summit opens as Philippines' parallel security agenda draws scrutiny
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-15 18:52:00
A security guard stands in the press centre during the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit in Manila on November 15, 2026. Photo: VCG The 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Meetings opened in Manila on Sunday, with Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. calling for regional unity and progress on a South China Sea Code of Conduct (COC), but he offered no clear timeline for concluding the long-awaited agreement. Against the backdrop of a planned Quad leaders' meeting in the Philippine capital, Chinese experts interviewed by the Global Times questioned whether Manila was using its ASEAN chairmanship to advance its own maritime security agenda rather than prioritizing regional consensus. Addressing the opening plenary, Marcos outlined three strategic priorities under the Philippines' ASEAN chairmanship - peace and security anchors, prosperity corridors, and people empowerment, according to the official Philippine News Agency. On the South China Sea, he called for advancing efforts toward an effective and substantive COC in accordance with international law, including the 1982 United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), local news site Philstar reported on Sunday. While Marcos pledged to complete 19 priority economic deliverables before Manila's chairmanship ends, he did not provide a deadline for the COC, which ASEAN foreign ministers had previously targeted for completion in 2026, according to Philstar. Gu Xiaosong, an expert on Southeast Asian studies, told the Global Times on Sunday that the Philippines' dual identity - serving as ASEAN chair while also being a claimant state in the South China Sea disputes - has amplified the duality in its actions. "As ASEAN chair, the Philippines is expected to promote regional cooperation and development, but as a claimant in the South China Sea, it also seeks to advance its own national interests," Gu said. Ding Duo, director of the Center for International and Regional Studies at the National Institute for South China Sea Studies, said Marcos' approach reflects a duality between his stated commitment to regional peace and Manila's expanding security cooperation with external powers. "While Manila talks about peace, stability and accelerating the COC negotiations, it continues to strengthen military and security cooperation with external powers such as the US, Japan and Australia," Ding told the Global Times on Sunday. Ding said the Philippines should use its ASEAN chairmanship to promote dialogue and regional unity rather than portray its own maritime positions as ASEAN's collective stance. "Manila should act as a bridge and promote unity, rather than use its chairmanship as a platform to pressure China," Ding said. At the invitation of President Marcos, Chinese Premier Li Qiang is scheduled to attend the 29th China-ASEAN Summit in Manila from November 15 to 16, according to a November 11 announcement carried by the Xinhua News Agency. China has consistently supported ASEAN centrality in the evolving regional architecture and advocated resolving differences in the South China Sea through dialogue and consultation. Beijing has also emphasized the importance of fully and effectively implementing the Declaration on the Conduct of Parties in the South China Sea (DOC) and advancing consultations on a COC, while promoting practical cooperation and maintaining peace and stability in the region. COC hurdles Foreign Secretary Maria Theresa Lazaro said on Saturday that approximately 77 percent of the paragraphs in the proposed COC had been agreed upon, while acknowledging that substantive issues remained unresolved. Lazaro declined to detail the remaining sticking points, deferring to an official announcement from ASEAN leaders during the 49th ASEAN Summit. A Southeast Asian diplomat involved in summit preparations told AFP that an agreement was not expected to be signed during the Manila summit. Philstar reported that outstanding differences include the COC's geographic scope, definitions of sensitive terms and whether the agreement should be legally binding. Gu said the Philippines, as ASEAN chair, should have made greater efforts to advance negotiations toward the targeted conclusion this year. "Although some 70 to 80 percent of the negotiations have reportedly been completed, the remaining 20 to 30 percent may prove the most difficult, as they involve substantive differences that will require considerable efforts to resolve," Gu said. He pointed out that different interpretations of the geographic scope could complicate efforts to establish a common framework, while sensitive terms require careful definition. "If the definition is too broad, it may be difficult for the parties to follow, but if it is too narrow, implementation could also become challenging," Gu said as he elaborated on the difficulties of translating general principles into workable rules. Another major challenge concerns whether the COC should be legally binding and how its provisions would be implemented, Gu noted. "If the COC is legally binding, the parties must determine how to ensure compliance. But without effective implementation mechanisms, it risks becoming little more than an extension of the existing DOC," he said. Ding said the COC should build on the DOC and focus on crisis management and practical cooperation. He warned that Manila's pursuit of closer military cooperation with external powers could undermine the political trust needed to advance negotiations. Quad challenges ASEAN centrality Leaders of the US, Japan, Australia and India are anticipated to meet in Manila on Tuesday, according to Reuters, citing two people familiar with the planning. The meeting would be the first Quad leaders' summit since September 2024 and the first since US President Donald Trump returned to office. Reuters reported that critical mineral supplies and the security of commercial shipping routes could feature on the agenda. Although the Quad members have maintained that the grouping is not directed against any particular country, it is widely viewed as a mechanism balancing China's regional influence. Gu said the timing of the Quad gathering illustrates how the Philippines is seeking to advance security priorities involving external powers alongside the ASEAN agenda. "The Quad meeting has little to do with ASEAN's own agenda, yet it has been arranged on the sidelines of the ASEAN summit," he said. Adding to the security-focused activities surrounding the ASEAN summit, AFP reported that an annual seminar on the South China Sea began on Sunday less than five kilometers from the main summit venue, with Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro, who was sanctioned by China earlier this year, delivering a keynote address. Ding warned that holding a Quad meeting alongside ASEAN-related gatherings could create a parallel security framework that risks weakening ASEAN's central role in regional affairs. He noted that ASEAN countries generally favor strategic autonomy and practical cooperation, rather than being drawn into confrontation between major powers. Despite the attention to security issues, the ASEAN summit also highlighted economic integration. Leaders are reportedly expected to tackle economic uncertainty and energy crises. Ding stressed that maritime disputes should not be allowed to overshadow the broader relationship between China and ASEAN. "Maritime disputes are only one aspect of China-Philippines relations, rather than a problem between China and ASEAN as a whole. Mutually beneficial cooperation remains the mainstream of China-ASEAN relations," Ding said. He called for continued adherence to a dual-track approach, under which disputes are addressed through negotiations by directly concerned countries, while China and ASEAN jointly maintain peace and stability in the South China Sea.
